title: Multi-timescale Microscopy Methods for the Characterization of Fluorescently-labeled Microbubbles for Ultrasound-Triggered Drug Release
protocol: Mix ultrapure water with 0.5 wt% casein in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS).
Add 1 wt% nanoparticles labeled with 0.21 wt% fluorescent dye NR668 to the mixture.
Ensure all steps are performed in a sterile glass crimp top vial.
Wear appropriate protective gear when handling nanoparticle solutions, including lab coat, goggles, and gloves.
Clean up any spills of nanoparticle solution immediately using 100% acetone.
Cap the vial with the rubber cap.
Mix slightly and place the vial in an ultrasonic bath for 10 min at room temperature.
Place a dispersion tool with the tip of the stirrer ~0.5 cm from the bottom of the glass vial.
Using a glass pipette, add perfluoropropane gas to the head space until the solution starts bubbling slightly.
Wrap self-sealing film around the base of the dispersion tool to prevent slipping during stirring.
Stir the solution vigorously at 1935 × g for 4 min using the dispersion tool.
Close the vial with the rubber cap and seal it for further use.
Store excess casein and nanoparticle solution at 4 °C.
Clean the dispersion tool with 100% acetone.
Turn a glass crimp top vial upside down to allow large bubbles to move away from the seal of the vial.
Insert a 19 G needle tip into the vial while it is upside down.
Remove a small amount of bubble suspension, approximately 0.2 mL.
Transfer the extracted suspension to a small tube for easier pipetting.
Dilute the microbubble suspension in filtered PBS using a pipette to achieve a concentration of 2 × 10^5 to 6 × 10^5 microbubbles/mL.
Wash the bubble suspension by diluting it in PBS, typically at a ratio of 1:100 (e.g., 100 µL of bubble solution in 10 mL of PBS).
Centrifuge the diluted suspension at speeds around 100 × g to separate microbubbles from free fluorescent dye.
Remove the supernatant containing microbubbles with a pipette for further analysis.
Discard the remaining solution which contains free fluorescent particles.
Repeat washing steps as necessary until free dye is minimized.
Add glycerol to the mixture to increase viscosity and reduce Brownian motion interference.
Switch on the confocal microscope.
Select a suitable objective and the desired laser and scanner for confocal microscopy.
Place the microbubble suspension in a chamber with thin walls for optimal imaging such as a channel slide.
Find a microbubble in bright-field.
Switch to confocal microscopy.
Set the desired top and bottom planes for scanning by the confocal microscope.
Acquire a Z-stack to observe the 3D structure using a step size of 100 nm in the Z-direction.
Attach a water-immersion objective with an appropriate magnification, working distance, and NA to the microscope.
Use a strobe light with a peak power output of at least 1 kW for illumination.
Use a tube lens between the microscope and the camera to minimize ambient light reaching the sensor of the high-speed camera.
Use a dimmable halogen light source for focusing on single microbubbles.
Use a programmable arbitrary waveform generator.
Connect a power-amplifier with 56 dB gain to drive the transducer.
Connect an oscilloscope to check the signal from the arbitrary waveform generator.
Connect a personal computer to program the acoustic pressure wave using an in-house script.
Set up a pulse/delay generator as the master trigger for synchronization.
Configure trigger delays on the pulse/delay generator and camera software.
Start recording 16 µs after ultrasound transmission to capture bubble oscillations.
Trigger the light source 1.5 µs before the start of recording for proper illumination.
Choose a suitable transducer with an appropriate center frequency.
Place the transducer in an opening of the water bath at an angle to minimize reflections from the sample holder membranes and reduce standing wave formation.
Calibrate the transfer function from voltage amplitude to pressure amplitude of the transducer using a fiber optic hydrophone as a function of the ultrasound transmit frequency.
Use a sample holder with optically and acoustically transparent membranes and a volume large enough to allow imaging of several single microbubbles within the same sample.
Place the cell culture cassette within the water bath for acoustic experiments.
Ensure the sample can be fully submerged and brought within the focus of both the transducer and the microscope objective.
Attach an aluminum support to a 3D micropositioning stage to move the sample holder independently.
Fill the water bath with water and switch on the dimmable halogen light source.
Attach a needle hydrophone (0.2 mm) to the sample holder arm.
Place the needle hydrophone in the water bath, with the tip in the field of view of the objective.
Turn on the amplifier and the arbitrary waveform generator.
Use single pulses of 5 to 10 ultrasound cycles and a pulse repetition frequency of 15 Hz.
Center and focus the hydrophone tip on the microscope image.
Move the tank in the XY-direction and the needle in the Z-direction until the maximum pressure amplitude is reached.
Adjust the focus of the microscope to refocus on the tip of the hydrophone.
Repeat steps for sample preparation.
Dilute the bubble solution to enable single-bubble imaging and rule out acoustic interactions with neighboring bubbles.
Open the outlet of the sample holder.
Inject the sample solution into the other opening until it is completely filled using a syringe.
Ensure there are no air bubbles inside the sample holder to prevent unwanted interactions with the ultrasound field.
Close both valves of the sample holder.
Place the sample holder perpendicular to the optical axis.
Keep the filled sample holder level to prevent shifting of the bubbles.
Program the desired ultrasound driving frequency and acoustic pressure in the arbitrary waveform generator through the in-house written script.
Move the sample holder containing the sample solution using the XYZ-stage to locate single microbubbles in the focus of the microscope.
Start with a field of view at a corner of the sample holder, ensuring that the edge of the microbubbles is clearly visible and in focus.
Attach the end of an optical fiber connected to the halogen light to a strobe light, while keeping the other end connected to the water bath.
Trigger the recording.
Move the cell culture cassette containing the microbubbles at least 2 mm from the previous location in the focal plane for each new experiment.
Repeat steps as many times as desired per ultrasound setting (frequency and acoustic pressure).
Empty the sample holder when the whole sample holder is insonified.
Refill the sample holder with fresh sample solution for subsequent experiments.
Adopt a programming environment to perform data analysis according to the research question.
Perform edge detection after processing the images.
Measure properties of image regions using a function.
Find the centroid of a bubble.
Calculate the derivative of the intensity profile around each bubble to detect the contour.
Extract relevant parameters from the radius over time for single microbubbles.
Build the setup for fluorescence microscopy with the same base used in bright-field microscopy.
Set the high-speed camera to record at 500,000 frames per second (400 x 250 pixels).
Record for 128 frames (256 µs).
Select a laser with an excitation wavelength of 532 nm and sufficient power for fluorescence imaging.
Couple the selected laser with an acousto-optic modulator.
Place a beam splitter, dichroic mirror, and notch filter between the laser and microscope objective.
Direct the excitation light towards the sample using the placed optical components.
Allow fluorescence emission to reach the camera through the setup.
Use a single-element, focused immersion transducer for insonification of microbubbles.
Set the transducer center frequency at 2.25 MHz with a focal distance of 1.88" and element diameter of 1".
Position the transducer at an angle of 35° relative to the optical axis.
Align the optical and acoustical systems as described in section 2.2.4.
Prepare the sample solution according to section 2.2.5 guidelines.
Set the desired ultrasound driving frequency on the arbitrary waveform generator through the in-house written script.
Set the acoustic pressure amplitude on the arbitrary waveform generator through the in-house written script.
Program a single burst of ultrasound consisting of 140 cycles with a 10-cycle Gaussian-tapered pulse.
Set the trigger delay for the laser for fluorescent excitation of nanoparticles from microbubbles during recording.
Move the sample holder containing the sample solution using the XYZ-stage to locate single microbubbles in the focus of the microscope.
Start with a field of view of a corner of the sample holder.
Trigger the recording.
Move the cell culture cassette containing microbubbles at least 2 mm from the previous location for each ultrasound setting.
Empty and refill the sample holder with fresh sample solution when insonifying the whole sample holder.
Analyze fluorescence microscopy recordings according to the research question.
Visually determine nanoparticle delivery for every microbubble observed.
Manually enter nanoparticle delivery occurrence into the programming environment if detachment and deposition are observed.
Acclimate the animals for one week before placing the window chambers.
Ensure that the weight of the mice is at least 22-24 g.
Anesthetize the animal by a subcutaneous injection of fentanyl (0.05 mg/kg)/medetomidine (0.5 mg/kg)/midazolam (5 mg/kg)/water (2:1:2:5) at a dose of 0.1 mL per 10 g weight.
Use a heating pad or a heating lamp to maintain the body temperature of the animal.
Pull gently on the double layer of skin on the back of the animal so that the skin is sandwiched between two symmetric polyoxymethylene frames of the window chamber.
Fix the chamber by placing two screws extending through the double skin layer and suturing along the upper edge of the chamber.
Remove the skin within the circular frame of the chamber on one side of the skin fold.
Place a cover glass with a diameter of 11.8 mm within the frame where the skin is removed to form a window into the tissue.
Use a subcutaneous injection of atipemazole (2.5 mg/kg), flumazenil (0.5 mg/kg), and water (1:1:8) at a dose of 0.1 mL per 10 g as antidote to terminate the anesthesia.
Place the animal in a heated recovery rack overnight.
Supplement the water for the animals with 25 mg/mL of enrofloxacin to prevent infection in the surgical site.
Maintain cancer cells at 37 °C in a 5% CO2 atmosphere.
Supplement culture medium with 10% fetal bovine serum, 100 U/mL penicillin, and 100 mg/mL streptomycin.
Anesthetize the animal by isoflurane (5% during induction and 1-2% during maintenance).
Remove the cover glass from the treatment site.
Apply 5 × 10^6 cancer cells in 30 µL of cell culture medium to the site.
Replace the cover glass after application of the cells.
Allow tumors to grow for 2 weeks before imaging.
Monitor the weight and health status of animals at least three times per week during tumor growth.
Perform intravital imaging during ultrasound treatment with a suitable microscope.
Use a multiphoton microscope equipped with a 20x water dipping objective (NA of 1.0, working distance of 2 mm).
Acquire images in resonant scanning mode at 31 frames per second with a field of view of 400 x 400 µm².
Use excitation wavelength of 790 nm for imaging.
Employ long-pass 590 nm and band-pass 525/50 nm filters for fluorescence detection.
Mount a suitable ultrasound transducer in a waveguide positioned below the objective at an angle of 45° with respect to the optical axis.
Fill the waveguide with distilled and degassed water.
Apply ultrasonic coupling gel on top of the waveguide.
Align the optical axis with the focus of the ultrasound.
Position a fiber-optic hydrophone in the focus of the objective.
Turn on the amplifier and the arbitrary waveform generator to excite the transducer with short bursts (5-10 cycles) at 100 Hz pulse repetition frequency.
Move the ultrasound transducer to the position where the highest pressure is detected with the hydrophone signal on the oscilloscope.
Position the heated animal holder connected to an XY-positioning stage between the waveguide and the objective.
Add more coupling gel to the setup.
Anesthetize the animal.
Place a tail vein catheter in the anesthetized animal.
Place the mouse in the heated holder.
Fix the window chamber in the holder.
Add a water droplet on top of the cover slip in the window chamber.
Move the objective into place to image the tumor tissue.
Inject fluorescently-labelled 2 MDa dextran intravenously (30 µL, 4 mg/mL diluted in saline) to visualize the vasculature.
Move the mouse using the XY-translation stage to find a position with suitable blood vessels.
Record baseline images before the ultrasound treatment.
Set the desired ultrasound driving frequency, pulse length, and acoustic pressure amplitude on the arbitrary waveform generator.
Inject 50 µL microbubbles (2 × 108 to 5 × 108 microbubbles/mL) intravenously.
Apply ultrasound while imaging.
Analyze images with open source image processing software.
Determine blood vessel parameters using the software.
Calculate diameter, branching, flow speed, and direction of blood vessels.
Evaluate accumulation of nanoparticles in the vessels.
Assess kinetics and penetration depth of extravasation of dextran into tumor tissue.
Measure kinetics and penetration depth of extravasation of nanoparticles into tumor tissue.
